source_text: Figmenta haec esse poetarum quidam putant ignorantes unde illa poetae acceperint, ac negant haec fieri posse: nec mirum est ita illis uideri. aliter enim quam res habet traditur a poetis: qui licet sint multo antiquiores quam historici et oratores et cetera genera scriptorum, tamen quia mysterium diuini sacramenti nesciebant et ad eos mentio resurrectionis futurae obscuro rumore peruenerat, eam uero temere ac leuiter auditam in modum commenticiae fabulae prodiderunt. et tamen idem testati sunt non auctorem se certum, sed opinionem sequi, ut Maro qui ait: sit mihi fas audita loqui. quamuis igitur ueritatis arcana in parte corruperint, tamen ipsa res eo uerior inuenitur, quod cum prophetis in parte consentiunt: quod nobis ad probationem rei satis est. errori tamen eorum subest ratio non nulla. nam cum prophetae adsiduis contionibus praedicarent iudicaturum esse de mortuis filium dei et haec adnuntiatio non lateret, quoniam rectorem caeli deum non alium putabant esse quam Iouem, iudicare aput inferos Iouis filium tradiderunt, sed tamen non Apollinem aut Liberum aut Mercurium, qui caelestes putantur, sed eum, qui et mortalis fuerit et iustus, uel Minoem uel Aeacum uel Rhadamanthum. corruperunt igitur poetica licentia quod acceperant, uel opinio ueritatem per diuersa ora sermonesque uarios dissipatam mutauit. nam quod peractis ad inferos mille annis rursus ad uitam restitui cecinerunt, Marone ita dicente: has omnis, ubi mille rotam uoluere per annos, Lethaeum ad fluuium deus euocat agmine magno, scilicet inmemores supera ut conuexa reuisant rursus et incipiant in corpora uelle reuerti, haec eos ratio fefellit, quod resurgent defuncti non post mille annos mortis suae, sed ut restituti rursus in uitam mille annis cum deo regnent. deus enim ueniet, ut orbe hoc ab omni labe purgato rediuiuas iustorum animas corporibus innouatis ad sempiternam beatitudinem suscitet. itaque praeter aquam obliuionis uera sunt cetera; quam idcirco finxerunt, ne quis illis opponeret: \'cur ergo non meminerint se aliquando uixisse aut qui fuerint aut quae gesserint?\' sed nihilominus tamen ueri simile non putatur et res tota uelut licenter ac fabulose ficta respuitur. nobis autem de resurrectione adfirmantibus et docentibus animas ad alteram uitam non oblitas sui, sed in eodem sensu ac figura esse redituras illut opponitur: \'tot iam saecula transierunt: quis umquam unus ab inferis resur- rexit, ut exemplo eius fieri posse credamus?\' at enim resurrectio fieri non potest dominante adhuc iniustitia. hoc enim saeculo necantur homines ui ferro insidiis uenenis et adficiuntur iniuriis egestate carceribus tormentis proscriptionibus. eo accedit quod iustitia inuisa est, quod omnes, qui deum sequi uolunt, non tantum odio habentur, sed uexantur omnibus contumeliis et excruciantur multiplici genere poenarum et ad inpios cultus manu factorum deorum non ratione aut ueritate, sed nefanda corporum laceratione coguntur. num lgitur oportet ad haec eadem resurgere aut reuerti homines ad uitam, in qua tuti esse non possunt? cum ergo iusti tam uiles habeantur, tam facile tollantur, quid putemus futurum fuisse, si & quis ab inferis rediens uitam postliminio recepisset? auferretur profecto ab oculis hominum, ne uiso eo uel audito deos uniuersi relinquerent et ad unius se dei cultum religionemque conuerterent. ergo semel fieri resurrectionem necesse est, cum malum fuerit ablatum, quoniam eos qui resurrexerint nec mori iam ulterius nec uiolari ullo modo fas est, ut beatam possint agere uitam quorum mors resignata est. poetae uero cum scirent hoc saeculum malis omnibus redundare, obliuionis amnem induxerunt, ne malorum ac laborum memores animae reuerti ad superos recusarent. unde Vergilius: o pater, anne aliquas ad caelum hinc ire putandum est sublimis animas iterumque ad tarda reuerti corpora? quae lucis miseris tam dira cupido? ignorabant enim quomodo aut quando id fieri oporteret, itaque ] renasci eas putauerunt et denuo ad uterum reuolui atque ad infantiam regredi. unde etiam Plato de anima disserens ex hoc ait posse cognosci animas esse inmortales atque diuinas, quod in pueris mobilia sint ingenia et ad percipiendum facilia, quod ea quae discant ita celeriter rapiant, ut non tunc primum discere illa uideantur, sed recognoscere atque reminisci: in quo uir sapiens poetis ineptissime credidit.
pass_a_gloss: These things are fictions of poets, some people think, being ignorant from where those poets received them, and they deny that these things can happen: and it is not wonderful that it seems so to them. For the poets hand down things otherwise than as they are: who, although they are much older than historians and orators and other kinds of writers, nevertheless, because they were ignorant of the mystery of the divine sacrament and the mention of future resurrection had come to them in obscure rumor, they rashly and lightly handed down what they had heard, in the manner of a fabricated story. And yet they themselves testified that they were not following a certain author, but an opinion, as Maro who says: let it be right for me to speak what I have heard. Although, therefore, they corrupted the secrets of truth in part, nevertheless, the thing itself is found to be more true, because they agree in part with the prophets: which is enough for us for proof of the thing. Nevertheless, a not insignificant reason underlies their error. For when the prophets were constantly preaching that the Son of God would judge the dead and this announcement was not hidden, because they thought that the ruler of heaven, God, was none other than Jupiter, they handed down that the son of Jupiter would judge in the underworld, but nevertheless, not Apollo or Liber or Mercury, who are thought to be heavenly, but him who was both mortal and just, either Minos or Aeacus or Rhadamanthus. Therefore, poetic license corrupted what they had received, or opinion changed the truth, which was dispersed through various mouths and various speeches. For what they sang, that after a thousand years had been completed, they would be restored to life again, Maro saying thus: when a thousand years have rolled by, God calls all these to the river Lethe in a great throng, so that, forgetful, they may revisit the world above and begin to wish to return to bodies again, this reasoning deceived them, because the dead will rise again, not after a thousand years of their death, but, having been restored, they will reign with God for a thousand years. For God will come, so that, having purified this world from all stain, he may raise the revived souls of the just, with their bodies renewed, to eternal blessedness. And so, except for the water of forgetfulness, the other things are true; which they fabricated for this reason, lest someone oppose them: 'why, therefore, do they not remember that they once lived or who they were or what they did?' But nevertheless, it is not thought to be like the truth, and the whole thing is rejected as if fabricated licentiously and in a fictional manner. But to us, affirming and teaching that souls are not forgetful of themselves, but will return to another life in the same sense and figure, this is opposed: 'so many ages have passed: who has ever risen from the underworld, so that we may believe it can happen, following his example?' But indeed, resurrection cannot happen while injustice still reigns. For in this age, men are killed by force, iron, ambushes, poisons, and are afflicted by injuries, poverty, prisons, torments, proscriptions. To this is added that justice is hated, that all who wish to follow God are not only hated, but are harassed by all insults and are tortured by multiple kinds of punishments, and are forced to impious worship of handmade gods, not by reason or truth, but by nefarious laceration of bodies. Should men, therefore, rise again or return to life, in which they cannot be safe? When, therefore, the just are considered so vile, so easily removed, what do we think would happen if someone returning from the underworld had received life again by restoration? He would certainly be taken away from the eyes of men, lest, having seen or heard him, all men would abandon their gods and convert to the worship and religion of the one God. Therefore, it is necessary that resurrection happen once, when evil has been removed, since it is not right that those who have risen again should die or be violated in any way, so that they may lead a blessed life, their death having been annulled. But the poets, since they knew that this age abounds with all evils, introduced the river of forgetfulness, lest the souls, mindful of evils and labors, refuse to return to the world above. Whence Vergil: 'O father, is it to be thought that some souls go from here to heaven and return again to sluggish bodies? What dire desire for light is this for wretched men?' For they were ignorant of how or when this should happen, and so they thought that they were reborn and returned again to the womb and regressed to infancy. Whence also Plato, discussing the soul, says from this that souls can be known to be immortal and divine, because in children, their talents are mobile and easy to perceive, because they seize what they learn so quickly, that they seem not to be learning it for the first time, but recognizing and remembering it: in which the wise man most foolishly believed the poets.

choices.english: These things are fictions of poets

pass_b_english: Some dismiss these accounts as mere poetic fictions, ignorant of the source from which the poets drew them, and deny that such things can happen. It is no wonder they see it that way. The poets transmit reality in a distorted form. Although they are far older than historians, orators, and other writers, they knew nothing of the mystery of the divine sacrament. The news of a future resurrection reached them only as an obscure rumor, and they rashly passed on what they had lightly heard as if it were a fabricated tale. Yet the poets themselves testified that they followed no single authoritative source, but general opinion — as Vergil says: 'May it be right for me to speak what I have heard.' Consequently, though they corrupted the secrets of truth in part, the matter itself proves more true because it agrees in part with the prophets; that partial agreement is sufficient for us as proof.

Nevertheless, a not insignificant reason underlies their error. The prophets had ceaselessly proclaimed that the Son of God would judge the dead, and this announcement was not hidden. Because the poets believed the ruler of heaven, God, was none other than Jupiter, they handed down that Jupiter's son would judge in the underworld. Yet they did not assign this role to Apollo, Liber, or Mercury, who are considered heavenly, but to one who was both mortal and just — either Minos, Aeacus, or Rhadamanthus. Thus poetic license corrupted what they had received, or opinion altered the truth after it had been dispersed through various mouths and speeches. They sang that after a thousand years souls would be restored to life again, Vergil saying: 'When a thousand years have rolled around, God calls them all in a great throng to the river Lethe, so that, forgetful, they may revisit the upper world and begin to wish to return to bodies.' This reasoning deceived them, because the dead will rise not after a thousand years of their death, but, once restored, will reign with God for a thousand years. God will come to purify this world from every stain and raise the revived souls of the just, with bodies renewed, to eternal blessedness. So, except for the water of forgetfulness, the other details are true. The poets invented that water for a reason: lest anyone object, 'Why then do they not remember that they once lived, or who they were, or what they did?' Even so, the whole account is not thought to resemble the truth and is rejected as if it were a licentious, fictional fabrication.

But when we affirm and teach that souls are not forgetful of themselves, but will return to another life in the same sense and figure, the objection is raised: 'So many ages have passed: who has ever risen from the underworld, that we might believe it can happen by his example?' Yet resurrection cannot happen while injustice still reigns. In this age men are killed by force, iron, ambushes, and poisons, and are afflicted by injuries, poverty, prisons, torments, and proscriptions. To this is added that justice is hated: all who wish to follow God are not only hated but harassed by every insult and tortured by multiple kinds of punishments, and are forced into the impious worship of handmade gods — not by reason or truth, but by nefarious laceration of their bodies. Should men therefore rise again or return to a life in which they cannot be safe? When the just are held so vile and so easily removed, what do we think would happen if someone returning from the underworld received life again by restoration? He would certainly be taken from the eyes of men, lest, seeing or hearing him, all would abandon their gods and convert to the worship and religion of the one God. Therefore resurrection must happen once, when evil has been removed, since it is not right that those who have risen should die again or be violated in any way, so that they may lead a blessed life whose death has been annulled.

The poets, since they knew this age abounds with every evil, introduced the river of forgetfulness so that souls, mindful of evils and labors, would not refuse to return to the world above. Hence Vergil: 'O father, is it to be thought that some souls go from here to heaven and return again to sluggish bodies? What dire desire for light is this for wretched men?' They were ignorant of how or when this should happen, and so they thought souls were reborn and returned again to the womb and regressed to infancy. Hence also Plato, discussing the soul, argues from this that souls can be known to be immortal and divine, because in children talents are mobile and easily perceived, and because they seize what they learn so quickly that they seem not to be learning it for the first time, but recognizing and remembering it. In this, a wise man most foolishly believed the poets.

review.notes: All clauses in the Latin source were checked against Pass A and Pass B. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation. Pass B provides a polished, segmented version that maintains the full semantic content, agency, and modality of the Latin. Scripture citations (Vergil, Plato, and the implied prophetic context) are handled correctly in both translations. No omissions or contradictions were found.

The translation accurately reflects the source text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key theological arguments. All quoted passages are correctly attributed, and the Latin text is fully translated without omissions or additions. The title 'Poets and Resurrection' appropriately captures the central theme of the passage.
